fixes.explanation: Oh, I wish it worked that way, friend, but it doesn't. God says, "Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken?" (Habakkuk 2:7). Creditors rising up is the opposite of forgetting. These folks are waking up, and I bet they brought their receipts.

Right, baker. The verse asks, "Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken? Then you will become their prey." (Habakkuk 2:7). Arising is the opposite of forgetting. Those who are owed wake up, and he becomes their prey.
That's the word, baker. "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain…" (Habakkuk 2:9). Notice the woe isn't aimed at the house itself. It's aimed at the unjust gain the house was built with.
I get why honest sounds like a nice word, baker. But the verse says, "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain…" (Habakkuk 2:9). The word there is unjust, and the woe is attached to it.

Neighbors aren't mentioned in this part, baker. The verse says, "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster!" (Habakkuk 2:9). He's hoping to get out of reach of disaster.

Yes, baker! "For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork." (Habakkuk 2:11). The walls he built are the ones that speak up. Then the rafters echo it from the woodwork. Picture building a house and then the bricks start talking.

True, baker. "Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity!" (Habakkuk 2:12). That's woe number three. The woe before it was about a house in verse 9, and this one is about a city.

That's the one, baker. "For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea." (Habakkuk 2:14). After all those woes, this verse hits like the oven door opening on a fresh batch. The earth gets filled with the knowledge of His glory.

Gold is a fair guess, baker, but it's not in the verse. God says, "…the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea." (Habakkuk 2:14). What fills the earth is the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.
Yes, baker. God says, "You will be filled with shame instead of glory." (Habakkuk 2:16). Shame takes the spot where glory was. That's a swap nobody would sign up for.

That's it, friend. "The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you…" (Habakkuk 2:16). He was pouring drinks for his neighbors, and now a cup is coming around to him. It's the LORD's right hand that holds it.
Correct, baker. God says, "For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). The violence against Lebanon is what overwhelms him. That's the place the verse names.

Egypt doesn't show up in this verse, friend. God says, "For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Egypt is the big name that jumps out, like the biggest cookie on the tray grabbing every hand. The verse names Lebanon, though.

Moab is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the name in this verse. God says, "For your violence against Lebanon will overwhelm you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Lebanon is the one that's named. Keep your eyes on the name the verse gives.
True, baker. God says, "…the destruction of animals will terrify you…" (Habakkuk 2:17). Terror is what comes to the proud man. This part is heavy, so I'll keep the jokes in the oven.

Right, baker. The verse says, "Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, yet there is no breath in it at all." (Habakkuk 2:19). Sprinkles on a cookie don't make it breathe, and gold doesn't either. The gold and silver cover the outside, and there's still no breath in it.
Yes, baker. "But the LORD is in His holy temple…" (Habakkuk 2:20). After all that talk of silent idols, this is the one who is there. The idols have gold on them, and there's no breath in them.
Not quite, friend. The verse says, "But the LORD is in His holy temple…" (Habakkuk 2:20). A high mountain sounds grand, but that's not what the verse says. It puts Him in His holy temple.

No city gate in this verse, baker. It says, "But the LORD is in His holy temple…" (Habakkuk 2:20). A city gate is a noisy spot, and this verse is headed toward silence. The LORD is in His holy temple, and then comes the call for all the earth to be quiet.

That's right, friend. "…let all the earth be silent before Him." (Habakkuk 2:20). I'll be honest, silence is hard for a guy with a mustache this talkative, but I'm working on it. All the earth is asked to be quiet, not just me.
